query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating an optimized content of tungsten carbide (WC) particles into the HEA matrix via spark plasma sintering will generate in-situ lubricious carbide phases (e.g., Co3W3C and Cr7C3) that reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a broad service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a predominantly single-phase FCC matrix that lacks engineered lubricious carbide phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce an optimized amount of WC particles into the HEA powder mix and sinter using SPS to promote in-situ formation of lubricious carbide phases.
generation.conditions: The intervention should remain effective under variable temperatures ranging from room temperature to high service temperatures (e.g., up to 600–800 °C) where both abrasive and oxidative wear mechanisms are active.
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formation and uniform dispersion of lubricious carbide phases (e.g., Co3W3C, Cr7C3) and well-dispersed WC particles that can form a protective tribo-film during sliding.
generation.mechanism: Optimized WC incorporation induces the formation of lubricious carbide phases during SPS, which not only act as reinforcing hard particles to enhance wear resistance but also form a low-friction tribo-film at contact interfaces, thereby reducing friction and mitigating wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated HEA matrix, the WC–HEA composite is expected to exhibit a noticeably lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate over the tested temperature range. While precise improvement values remain uncertain, prior evidence indicates significant enhancement in wear resistance and tribological performance.
generation.baseline: Pure HEA matrix material processed under identical conditions without WC addition.
generation.boundary: Exceeding the optimal WC content (e.g., >30 vol.%) may lead to excessive formation of Cr-rich phases and interface bonding issues that could negate the lubricity benefits, while too little WC may not produce sufficient carbide phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in the coefficient of friction and wear rate depend on the WC content and processing conditions; the optimal WC level and long-term stability of the lubricious tribofilm under cyclic loading still require further determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of pure HEA matrix and another set with an optimized WC addition via SPS. Conduct tribological tests (e.g., pin-on-disk or sliding wear tests) across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Compare the coefficient of friction and wear rate of both sample sets under identical testing conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (CoF) at multiple set temperatures
Wear volume or wear scar depth/area
Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, XRD) to confirm the formation of lubricious carbide phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the WC-incorporated HEA composite does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the pure HEA across the tested temperature range, or if the expected lubricious carbide phases do not form as confirmed by microstructural characterization.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. The Effect of WC Content on Properties of Composites
cited_evidence.text: The strengthening mechanisms of WC particle-reinforced HEA matrix composites mainly include the second phase strengthening of the hard phase itself, the dislocation strengthening introduced by the difference in thermal expansion coefficients between the hard phase and the matrix, the fine grain strengthening of the matrix grains by the hard phase during the ball milling process, and solid solution strengthening caused by diffusion of W and C atoms [,].

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. The Effect of WC Content on Properties of Composites
cited_evidence.text: WC particles have high hardness, good wear resistance, strong resistance to deformation during friction, and are less prone to plastic deformation, resulting in increased friction resistance and stronger wear resistance of the composites. With the increase of WC content, the wear mechanism of HEA matrix composites changes from adhesive wear to abrasive wear, and the formation of second phases such as Cr-rich and Co3W3C carbides in the composites also reduces the wear volume, which is beneficial to the improvement of wear resistance of HEA matrix. When the WC content increases to 30%, the WC content is too much, resulting in an excessive amount of the Cr-rich phase being generated in the composite, leading to more prominent interface problems, affecting the bonding between the hard phase and the matrix, resulting in a poor overall lubrication effect and increased friction coefficient of the composite. However, overall, compared with the Cr-rich phase, the distribution of WC particles in the 30 WC–HEA sample is more dispersed, and the effect of WC is more prominent. reading.lever: Optimized WC particle incorporation into HEAs via SPS to generate in-situ lubricious carbide phases.
reading.why: This intervention, demonstrated in related HEA composites, directly addresses friction and wear challenges by forming self-lubricating tribofilms over a wide temperature range.
